newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND FACES CAREER DILEMMA.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND FACES CAREER DILEMMA.

text.p: It took Luc Alphand a lot of time and pain to have a first taste of success.
Now the 31-year-old Alpine skier from Serre-Chevalier, who had to wait until he reached his thirties and his seventh World Cup season to win, faces a dilemma.
It took the Frenchman so long to reach his peak that he is tempted to make it last as long as possible, or at least until next year's Nagano Olympics.
But he also feels the pressures of being a family man.
"I will take time to decide about my future. I'd love to stop at 32 with fond memories of my last season," he said.
"To go on the road again would mean leaving my house and my kids. I know that a lot of people would like me to go on, thinking I could win more races. But it is not as simple as that," he said.
"First of all, you need not be injured."
Alphand should know as the World Cup circuit has held something of an injury jinx for him.
The last of a long string of injuries -- he tore his knee ligaments on Whistler Mountain, British Colombia, in 1993 -- almost ended his career. He still thinks about it at times.
"I nearly fell in Chamonix and it was scary. For a fraction of a second, the pictures of Whistler came back to mind," he said.
That is why Alphand does not feel like risking competing a season too many.
But there is one race which will certainly help him make a decision: the downhill at the world championships in Sestriere.

"I said at the start of the season that if I should win only one race this season, it should be the Sestriere downhill. Now I'd say that if I were to win but one more, I'd like it to be this one too."
It is true that the easy-going Frenchman is almost a local here, living but 35 kms away from Sestriere on the other side of the Montgenevre pass.
"I know the piste well. It's almost like home," added the current World Cup leader, who was downhill junior world champion on the same piste almost 15 years ago.

And Italy has seemed to inspire the Frenchman this season as he won the two downhills held in the country, in Bormio and Val Gardena. The nearness of home without the pressure of national media and fans has seemed to help.
For many, Italian Kristian Ghedina, who also won three downhills this season and has, like Alphand, seen his career nearly brought to a halt by a crash, may be his main rival.
"Home pressure will be enormous for Ghedina. But pressure often makes him better," Alphand said.
If he has already left his mark as the best French downhill specialist since Jean-Claude Killy, Alphand would earn an even greater stature should he win here.

He would then become the first Frenchman to win a world title since Michel Vion, now his team boss, won the combined crown in Schladming in 1982 and the first to win the blue riband event since Killy in 1968.
But since scoring his first career victory in a super-G in Laax on Wednesday, Alphand can now set sights on a double he would be the first-ever skier to achieve.
